39.0.s.en: (1) Murmuring and the vanity of toil

39.0.0.en: 1- “I said, I will take heed to my ways, that I sin not with my tongue: I will keep my mouth with a muzzle, while the wicked is before me.”

39.0.1.en: 1- When David saw the success and strength of the wicked, he was troubled within himself and almost spoke words of murmuring, but by the power of God he was able to restrain his tongue from sin.

39.0.2.en: 2- David's restraint of his tongue enabled him not to fall into evil conduct, since evil speech gives birth to evil deeds. Thus David's taking heed to his way enabled him to control his tongue, his thoughts and his actions.

39.0.3.en: 3- This verse shows a dialogue within David's soul, that is, he holds himself to account before God so that he may not slip into his faults.

39.0.4.en: 4- This verse shows the danger of the tongue, which is able to kindle evil within the whole being of man and in his deeds, so that it needs a muzzle, as though the tongue were a predatory beast that of necessity needs restraint, especially when it is provoked by the events of life and the conduct of the wicked.

39.0.5.en: 5- David's tongue was liable to condemn the wicked, or to justify himself, or to murmur against God. It was exposed to many faults, from which David was able to free himself, even if he had fallen into them in thought or in heart; yet this shows David's striving and his attempt to control himself.

39.0.6.en: 6- David's taking heed to his way, that is, his control of his thoughts and conduct, also made his tongue unable to err, because out of the abundance of the heart the tongue speaks; so when his inside became pure, his speech became pure.

39.0.7.en: 7- David feels that the wicked man is before him and not against him, so David does not treat him as an enemy or condemn him, but only feels that the wicked man is different from him in his conduct in evil. Therefore David keeps a loving heart toward him and prays for him; indeed he was gentle toward his son Absalom, although Absalom wanted to kill David. Thus David charged Joab, the commander of his army, to deal gently with Absalom.

39.1.0.en: 2- “I was dumb with silence, I held my peace, even from good; and my sorrow was stirred.”

39.1.1.en: 1- David was able to control his tongue and keep silent, so he did not sin with an evil word; and he also held his peace from good speech, so he did not say a kind word. Yet the distress was still within him, that is, in his thoughts and feelings, and he continued to suffer from these pains until his heart grew calm.

39.1.2.en: 2- David's silence is a great striving that God praises, but he was not able to do good to the wicked man who was before him, and so the pain continued within him.

39.1.3.en: 3- If a man keeps silent from hearing the voice of God, he will lose his ability to do good, and so the pains of sin stir within him.

39.1.4.en: 4- When Shimei cursed David, David kept silent and did not answer him, whether by words or by allowing Joab to kill him; but he held his peace from doing good or speaking kindly, and then David blamed himself and suffered, because his love toward Shimei was not perfect, since he ought to have been silent about the evil and also to speak good in the face of Shimei's curses.

39.1.5.en: 5- David kept silent from evil speech, but he was not able to speak good, since the wicked man does not accept good speech; so there was a struggle within David, and pains because he was unable to speak the word of God, for the wicked man refuses to hear holy speech.

39.2.0.en: 3- “My heart was hot within me, while I was musing the fire burned: then spake I with my tongue:”

39.2.1.en: Musing (lahaji): repeating the thought or the speech.

39.2.2.en: 1- When the wicked wronged David, his heart was moved within him, and he was distressed because they wronged him while he was innocent. Then the thoughts were repeated within him until his heart was kindled with distress at those who wronged him. Finally he spoke with his tongue and rebuked them for their wrong to him although he was innocent, as he rebuked King Saul twice when Saul fell into David's hand and he did not harm him (1 Sam 24:11; 26:23).

39.2.3.en: 2- This verse may also mean that David's heart, when it heard the wrongs of the wicked toward him, had pity on them because they sinned against God; for he wants the salvation of all and loves even the one who wrongs him. Prayers for those who wronged him were repeated within David until his heart almost burned with the fire of love for them. And David's tongue spoke about the wrongdoer, or to him, seeking an excuse for him, as he did with Shimei the son of Gera, when he declared that Shimei's wrong was a divine direction to David (2 Sam 16:10).

39.2.4.en: 3- There is a third interpretation of this verse, which is that when David heard the wrongs directed against him, he was distressed by them, and his heart grew hot within him because of them. But he turned his heart to God in prayer, asking His help, and was kindled in crying out to God to deliver him and comfort him, and David's attachment to God increased. David's occupation with speaking to God made him keep silent, so he did not answer the wrong of the wicked with any word of wrong, because God gave him peace and tranquility, and even forgiveness. So he was content with his speaking to God with his tongue and with the prayers of love for God that drew his heart, and he left off thinking about the wrongs of others.

39.3.0.en: 4- “LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is: that I may know how frail I am.

39.3.1.en: 1- David asks God to make him know that his life on earth is short and will end and he will pass away from the earth, and so he is not troubled by the wrongs of the wicked but bears them, because they are temporary and will end with the end of his life on earth, and in place of them he will receive heavenly glories.

39.3.2.en: 2- David feels that the afflictions he passes through have an end, so he asks God to make him know their end and the number of their days, and how he will pass away from the earth; and so he hastens to acquire virtue and to do good in preparation for eternity, and is not occupied with the wrongs of others, but is even able to let the wrongs push him to repent of his sins and to cling to God and eternity. David does not ask to know the number of his days on earth, or the days of his trial precisely, but he wants God to remind him that his days are limited, so that he may be occupied with eternity.

39.4.0.en: 5- “Behold, thou hast made my days as an handbreadth; and mine age is as nothing before thee: verily every man at his best state is altogether vanity. Selah.”

39.4.1.en: 1- As David looks toward eternity, he sees that his life is very short, which he expresses as handbreadths, not a long period, but a breath and not a great wind, and then he sees it as nothing, for the days of life pass and are not remembered afterward. Thus this leads to David's humility and his non-attachment to material things, as he feels that he is a stranger on the earth.

39.4.2.en: 2- As David feels the shortness of his life on earth, indeed that it is nothing in itself, he is careful to live with God so that his life may have value and extend into eternity in unspeakable happiness.

39.5.0.en: 6- “Surely every man walketh in a vain shew: surely they are disquieted in vain: he heapeth up riches, and knoweth not who shall gather them.”

39.5.1.en: 1- David likens the life of man to a phantom and not a tangible reality, and to loud noises (tumult) that then end, and you cannot hold on to them. Also man hoards many material treasures, then dies and takes nothing of them. Therefore the wise man does not cling to this passing world and all his possessions.

39.5.2.en: 2- This world is full of tumult, that is, disturbance, and the wise man is the one who lives with God, so his heart is filled with peace, and indeed he possesses God within him, so his life becomes a true reality and not a phantom, and he increases in the knowledge of God and every virtue instead of the passing material things. And thus every day he prepares for eternity in which he will remain.

39.5.3.en: May the sojourning of the world be fixed in your heart, so that you do not waste your time in argument and quarrels with others over passing things, and be careful to possess God within you through many prayers.

39.6.0.en: 7- “And now, Lord, what wait I for? my hope is in thee.

39.6.1.en: As David sees the vanity of the world and its passing, and that the life of man is short and will end, he therefore waits for nothing in the passing world, but the only One whom he waits for is God. He is the only hope in this life, that man may live with Him, and He alone remains forever; so he hopes in Him and places all his hopes in Him.

39.7.0.en: 8- “Deliver me from all my transgressions: make me not the reproach of the foolish.”

39.7.1.en: 1- The sins and transgressions that man commits separate him from God, so he loses God's presence in his life. Therefore David asks God to deliver him from his transgressions, and thus he becomes pure and worthy for God to dwell in him, and he enjoys fellowship with Him.

39.7.2.en: 2- Transgressions cause Satan, who is the foolish one, and all who follow him, who are the wicked, to rejoice at the fall of the righteous. So David asks God to forgive him his sins even if he needs divine discipline, but God must take his sins away from him, so that the foolish one may not rejoice at David's fall, and thus David may not go to eternal torment, but on the contrary may have enjoyment with God in the Kingdom.

39.8.0.en: 9- “I was dumb, I opened not my mouth; because thou didst it. 10- Remove thy stroke away from me: I am consumed by the blow of thine hand.”

39.8.1.en: 1- David submits to God in all His disciplines, because David is repentant and submissive to the will of God, so he keeps silent and accepts all God's arrangements for his life. Thus he enjoys God's guidance of him and His care for him.

39.8.2.en: 2- David expresses his suffering from God's discipline of him, so he begs Him to remove His stroke from him, that is, His disciplines, whether they were wrongs from others, or God's forsaking him so that he was exposed to falling into sins; he begs God to stop His stroke upon him and to have pity on him, because he is very weary, until he is near to perishing. By this humbling before God, David obtains His forgiveness, His love and His care.

39.9.0.en: 11- “When thou with rebukes dost correct man for iniquity, thou makest his beauty to consume away like a moth: surely every man is vanity. Selah.”

39.9.1.en: 1- When God allows disciplines for His children so that they may repent, He makes them feel that the world is passing; for as the moth consumes woolen clothes and possessions, so God consumes the desires and possessions of man, so that he may not cling to the world, and may feel that his life is short and small, like a breath, and so becomes a stranger to the world and clings to God.

39.9.2.en: 2- Because of the importance of being a stranger to the world, David places a musical pause, which is the word Selah, after this verse, as it was placed after the fifth verse of this psalm, to confirm the sojourning of the world within the heart of everyone who chants this psalm.

39.10.0.en: 12- “Hear my prayer, O LORD, and give ear unto my cry; hold not thy peace at my tears: for I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner, as all my fathers were.”

39.10.1.en: 1- At the end of the psalm David begs God to listen to his prayer and his crying out, and even if he is unable to speak and express himself, God looks upon his tears and intervenes, removes his pains and forgives his sins. For David feels that his sins are the cause of God's disciplines and of all his pains.

39.10.2.en: 2- David also begs God to answer him, because he is a stranger in the earth, like his fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who lived in tents as strangers all their days on earth. And because the stranger has no attachment to earthly things, his hope is his relationship with God and his eternity.

39.11.0.en: 13- “O spare me, that I may recover strength, before I go hence, and be no more.”

39.11.1.en: Recover strength (atabalaj): from the breaking of dawn, that is, the appearing of the light of dawn and the rising of the sun; the intended meaning is that I may shine forth, find rest and be enlightened.

39.11.2.en: 1- The repentant David accepted God's discipline in all the pains he passes through, but he felt the weight of the pains upon him, so he asked God to remove His disciplining hand from him, that he may find rest and his life may shine anew, and so enjoy his life with God before his age comes to an end.

39.11.3.en: 2- In the Hebrew original the word “spare” means “forgive,” so David wants God to assure him that He has forgiven his sins; then his face will shine and he will rejoice before he leaves this world.

39.11.4.en: You have boldness with God as His child, so ask of Him, indeed persist with Him to hear your prayer, and support you and give you rest, and delight you with His presence with you, so that your hope may be renewed and your faith in Him made firm.

39.11.5.en: Cry for help and longings: “Judge me, O Lord, and plead my cause” (v. 1) Introduction:

39.11.6.en: 1- Most students of the Holy Bible see that this psalm is a continuation of the previous psalm, that is, the two psalms were one psalm that was divided. This psalm must have been written by David, because before David the Tabernacle was not in Jerusalem, and there were not two dwellings of God, “Thy tabernacles” (v. 3); and after David, that is, in the time of Solomon, there was one temple built in Jerusalem, and there were not two dwellings, or two tents.

39.11.8.en: When Jonathan, the son of Saul, saw the evil in his father's heart toward David, he warned David to flee so that no harm would befall him. This was mentioned in the title of this psalm in the Septuagint.

39.11.9.en: 3- This psalm expresses the sufferings that David expects from Saul, and asks God's help to rescue him and bring him back from the places to which he fled, that he may enjoy worship in the temple of God.

39.11.10.en: 4- This psalm expresses the feelings of every person surrounded by threats and problems, whose hope is firm in God, and whose longings are bound to the Church and her sacraments.

39.11.11.en: 5- This psalm is a prophecy about the captives in the Babylonian captivity, who are surrounded by idolaters and long to return to Jerusalem, to enjoy the worship of God in His temple.

39.11.12.en: 6- This psalm is also a prophecy about Christ, whom the Jews surrounded, trying to kill Him, but His hope was firm that He would accomplish the redemption of mankind, and die for it, then rise, to raise it up in Himself.

39.11.13.en: 7- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of the Third Hour, because it speaks about the Holy Spirit who enlightens the lives of the children of God and guides them to worship Him in the Church (vv. 3, 4).
